item.title: Iran offers to mediate as Saudi-Houthi conflict escalates
item.description:
Iran offers to mediate as Saudi-Houthi conflict escalates

Iran has urged Saudi Arabia to avoid a military approach and pursue a political solution to its escalating conflict with Yemen’s Houthi group, offering to help facilitate dialogue after deadly attacks on Saudi airports intensified regional tensions.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi made the offer during a telephone call with Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan on Sunday, according to statements reported by the Saudi state news agency and Iranian media.

“Insisting on a military approach and disregarding a political solution would only further complicate the situation,” Araghchi said. 

The region’s crises had no military solutions, he said, adding that Tehran was ready to provide assistance to facilitate dialogue between Saudi Arabia and Yemen and help achieve a political settlement. 

Read more: Iran offers to mediate as Saudi-Houthi conflict escalates

item.title: Who are Yemen's Houthis and what do they want?
item.description:
Who are Yemen's Houthis and what do they want?

Officially known as Ansar Allah, or "helpers of God", the movement emerged in Yemen's far north in the 1990s around the cleric Hussein al-Houthi.

It is rooted in Zaydism, a branch of Shia Islam whose followers are a minority in Yemen but concentrated in the northern highlands.

The group fought six rounds of war with the government of former president Ali Abdullah Saleh between 2004 and 2010. Hussein al-Houthi was killed in the first and leadership passed to his brother, Abdul-Malik al-Houthi, who still heads the movement.

IRGC official warns against foreign powers interfering in Hormuz Strait

item.description:

  • Follow our Australia politics live blog for latest updates

  • Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

An International Monetary Fund scenario where global oil prices jump to US$130 a barrel over coming months could push Australian petrol prices up by another 30 cents per litre and pile pressure on the Reserve Bank to hike interest rates, economists say.

In its latest World Economic Outlook, the IMF modelled the impact on global growth and inflation from a worsening Middle East crisis that extended into next year, highlighting the “clear and present danger” to a resilient global economy from turmoil in commodity and bond markets.

item.title: Saudi Arabia further suspends flights after latest deadly Houthi attack on airport
item.description:
Energy minister says ‘fear has no place in the Saudi lexicon’ as paramilitary group again breaches stretched defences

  • Why are the Houthis attacking Saudi airports and how are the missiles getting through?

Saudi Arabia has been forced to suspend all flights to and from its main international airport in Riyadh until next Saturday after a further round of Houthi missile attacks caused more damage and left one person dead. Some airlines, including Gulf Air and Bahrain Air, had already said they were cancelling flights until next Saturday. More missiles were fired at Saudi Arabian cities by the Houthis on Monday, Saudi Arabian’s military spokesperson said.

The Gulf nation announced it was suspending flights from Riyadh, its second busiest airport, after Houthi missiles killed 13 people on Saturday and left more than 300 injured. Saudi state TV broadcast CCTV footage that showed passengers deluged in smoke and falling masonry as they queued at the airport terminal to board a plane just as the Houthi missile struck.
